To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rates of acquisition of a spatial memory task and the decay of long-term enhancement of synaptic strength are slower in aged rats than in young rats, and that the relative differences in the two rates of aging are similar in the two measures.

(1) old rats learn the Morris water maze problem more slowly, (2) old rats forget what they have learned more quickly, and (3) these age-related differences are paralleled by age-related differences in the rates at which hippocampal synaptic enhancement is increased by high-frequency stimulation and at which the enhanced synapses return to their baseline level of activity

the age difference in the rate of learning a spatial problem is related to an age difference in the speed with which hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP) develops, and the age difference in retention of the problem is related to the rate at which LTP decays.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of aging on learning and memory.
the question of whether the rate of acquisition and forgetting in a particular behavioral task is related to the rates of increase or decay of a particular synaptic mechanism.
the effects of aging on memory and synaptic plasticity, with the goal of determining the extent to which these effects are due to changes in the mechanisms of memory and learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate of learning is slower and the rate of forgetting is faster in aged rats than in young animals.
the data support the hypothesis that LTE is a mechanism underlying learning and memory.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate of acquisition of spatial memory in old animals is slower than in young animals, but the rates of forgetting of spatial memory are similar.
the rates of behavioral acquisition, forgetting, and long-term synaptic enhancement in hippocampal synapse are similar in young and old animals.
age-related deficits in spatial learning and memory are associated with a deficit in hippocampal synaptic plasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the rates of behavioral acquisition, forgetting and LTE increase and decay are very similar across age, suggesting that LTE is a good model for the underlying mechanism of spatial learning and memory.
the rate of forgetting is a good measure of the rate of decay of synaptic enhancement.
the age-related changes in synaptic enhancement are very much similar to the age-related changes observed in the performance of a spatial memory task.
